The following is an abridged version of the commencement address given by former Ambassador Jeff Bleich at Piedmont High School’s graduation ceremony on June 2 at Witter Field. My great grandparents faced persecution and poverty in Eastern Europe for years. At some point, they decided that even if their life elsewhere would be no better, they owed it to their children and grandchildren to at least try. They left behind everything they had, everyone they knew and loved, to come to America. Their family members who remained, our ancestors in Europe, perished in the Holocaust. I do not have heirlooms, or pictures, or distant cousins I can find on 23andMe. The only place our family exists is in America. It was the one nation that let my great-grandparents in and gave them a chance. So I owe a debt to my great grandparents and to the people who welcomed them. Know this: I would not be alive today were it not for the courage of my ancestors, and the courage of people from this country who were willing to take them in. Each day is the gift that others’ courage gave me. We don’t stand on the shoulders of giants. We stand on the shoulders of people just like us – people who struggle with these decisions and who are uncertain. But in the end, they had a choice, and they chose to take risks and sacrifice for a greater good. And all they expected from us is to do the same. articles.text: Report finds $500,000 will be cost of full electrification Piedmont Connect, a community organization that supports city efforts on sustainability, released a newsletter on June 6 praising the city for moving forward with an all-electric aquatic facility. “We are proud that our Council unanimously voted for an all-electric facility, powered by an on-site solar PV-thermal array, electric heat pumps, and supplemental clean electricity from East Bay Community Energy (EBCE), our county’s Electrical Energy Aggregator,” said Piedmont Connect Board Member Hope Salzer. “Our new aquatics facility will produce no greenhouse gas pollution directly, a significant step towards the City’s goal of municipal facilities and activities emitting no fossil pollution by 2050.” The organization anticipated that city council’s commitment to electrifying the aquatic facility will also inspire community members to electrify their homes. City Council unanimously approved the plan to proceed with full electrification of the pool at an April 4 meeting. However, City Administrator Sara Lillevand noted at the time that upfront construction costs for the project could reach $500,000, according to an updated energy use report. These costs include eighteen heat pump chillers, four heat exchangers, and HVAC related items, including seismic work, hauling and other building-related HVAC scope. Lillevand proposed proceeding with the project, and seeking additional funding from outside sources. City Council adopted a policy entitled “acceptance of donations and naming of city owned facilities” at a meeting on May 2. The purpose of the policy is to encourage public-private partnerships that provide donations to support and enhance city services and facilities, which will help fund the all-electric facility. articles.text: Teacher wages, girls’ athletics a low priority for Piedmont School Board Editor: Piedmont School District has a priorities problem. On May 11th, scores of teachers testified to the school board that inadequate teacher pay is the key factor in the frequent teacher turnover at PUSD. They seek a reasonable cost of living adjustment. On May 25th, Piedmont’s female athletes and coaches presented the board with details of PUSD’s deficient Title IX funding and disparate treatment of female athletes. These were very moving presentations on high priority matters, and yet our school board obsessively focuses attention and funding on Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging (DEIB) initiatives. The latest of many examples of the school district’s misplaced priorities is last week’s creation and funding of a high school class to teach BIPOC (Black Indigenous People of Color) students how to “mentor” other BIPOC students in our elementary and middle schools. Many of us agree that including some DEI-B content into the curriculum is appropriate, but clearly, using PUSD’s limited funds to teach “mentoring” solely for BIPOC students is not a current priority compared to funding adequate teacher pay or fulfilling Title IX legal obligations. And let’s not forget that the high school still doesn’t have AP courses for physics, chemistry, or robotics, raising the question once again of misplaced priorities. I believe our school board needs to adjust its priorities toward academic excellence, recruitment and retention of excellent teachers, and meeting its Title IX legal obligations. If you agree, email the PUSD board at: schoolboard@ piedmont.k12.ca.us.

articles.text: Oakland resident Sara Paul and a team of volunteers developed and operate a smart phone application that delivers information on high-risk vegetation fires and wildfires that have the potential to become high-risk. Watch Duty launched in August 2021 in Sonoma, Napa, and Lake counties. Two weeks ago, the app expanded to include all 58 counties in California. An interactive map shows where wildfires are burning across the state in real-time with information gathered from a variety of channels and agencies. “Watch Duty fills important gap – a source of reliable fire information provided in a timely manner,” said Paul. “Everyone who is involved in the fire reporting side of our app – about 15 of us – have been sharing and reporting information about fires on other [social media] platforms like Facebook and Twitter. But let’s face it, social media is a horrible place to have to troll through to get information that might save your life.” The app was created by John Clarke Mills. Paul explained that Mills created the platform after his own experience searching for information on his ranch in Sonoma County - which has been in the radius of wildfire danger multiple times over the past three years. articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew members prepare pancakes for the 4th of July Parade. Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade will be anchored once again by the community pancake breakfast served by the Piedmont Community Service Crew in the Veterans Hall from 8:00 to 10:30 a.m. Guests will be serenaded with the music of the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band playing music at the front of the building. The Pancake Breakfast is organized completely by the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a youth-led coed Venturing Crew, part of the Piedmont Scouts, founded in 2004 and still led by Ken Li. The entire event is youth-run from start to finish. Crew members Klara Zietlow and Madelyn Hill, who serve as co-Vice Presidents of Fundraising, have the task of soliciting donations from Village Market and Piedmont Grocery which have long supported the event. “There’s a lot of work that goes into it. Right after the girls were elected in spring, they had to work quickly. Planning for the pancake breakfast, typically begins months in advance,” Li said. In addition to flipping flapjacks and serving them to a large crowd, crew members will be serving sausages, fresh fruit, orange juice and coffee. All food is freshly prepared. Prior to COVID, the group would serve over 400 plates of breakfast before the parade. The crew uses proceeds from the pancake breakfast to support their philanthropic projects, which includes service work in partnership with Rebuilding Together Oakland to renovate the homes of low-income and elderly Oakland residents. Each year, PCSC raises over $12,000 with the help of fundraisers like this and parent donations. “It’s nice that PCSC has this very positive standing and respect [in the community]. And the teams feel really proud of that, which spurs them to do a great job,” Li said. “On a typical project, we’ll spend a few thousand dollars on materials. We plan, execute and fund the projects.” Advance tickets to the breakfast are available on the Piedmont BSA website at: https://www. piedmontbsa.org/events/july-4thpancake-breakfast/. For those who cannot join the breakfast, but would like to donate to the Community Service Crew, visit https://rtoakland.org/ blog/pcsc.

articles.text: The Alameda County Fair returns this summer at the Fairgrounds in Pleasanton. It is the seventh largest in California and will take place June 17 through July 10 at the Alameda County Fairgrounds, located at 4501 Pleasanton Avenue. A plethora of events will transpire over the course of three weeks, including the Alaskan Racing Pigs, musical events, movies on the lawn, carnival rides and a “drone show.” The fair will be open 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily, and carnival hours are Wednesday through Sunday. Concerts are scheduled every night at 8 p.m. The fair kicks off on Friday, June 17, and admission is free that day until 3 p.m. On Saturday, June 18 at 3:30 p.m., Nathan’s Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest will host its only West Coast event. For more details, and to purchase tickets, visit www.alamedacountyfair.com. Consider signing up as a volunteer. Nearly 900 volunteers of all ages help out at the fair each year. Organizations that volunteer include local schools and colleges, youth groups, garden clubs, Girl Scout troops, and performing arts groups. articles.text: A bike path in Piedmont. The city will move forward with a bike lane on Moraga Avenue as recommended by the Piedmont Pedestrian and Bicycle Committee last year, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed. Recommendations made by the committee considered survey responses and suggestions from the community, which culminated in the Safer Streets plan. The Safer Streets plan was adopted by city council on December 6, 2021. The plan was launched in November 2014 to identify sites and make recommendations to make the city more pedestrian- and bike-friendly. The proposed bike lane, a high priority item in the Plan, will complete the bike lane improvements on Moraga Avenue. A current bike lane on Moraga Avenue exists between Ramona and Bonita Avenues, and between Bonita and the City limit to the east. The new project will be a Class 2 bike lane, generally five-feet wide, established along streets and defined by pavement striping and signage. The new bike lane would be on the uphill direction from Red Rock Road to the city limits. Plans for the project will be reviewed by Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. It is estimated to go out to bid in late July and awarded in August, Gonzales confirmed, with construction anticipated to begin in September.

articles.text: For the 19th year, the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band will take a lead position in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade, with its parasol-toting, shuffle-stepping Grand Marshal leading the way. Zenith, a Berkeley-based group, lays claim to being the most authentic brass band playing the music of old New Orleans from the formative years of 100 years ago to the present. Parade bands in New Orleans are still part of the musical tradition in the Crescent City, playing for funerals, parades, picnics and dances. All members of the Zenith band have been playing in similar jazz bands in the Bay Area for many years. Its Grand Marshal leads the way, proudly holding a fringed parasol, wearing a colorful sash, and doing a shuffle step down the length of Highland Avenue. People dancing behind the band, sometimes swirling parasols, are known as the second line. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band has been a major attraction for many years at the New Orleans By the Bay production at Shoreline Amphitheater. It has been part of the Traditional Jazz portion of the Concord Jazz Festival for 17 years, and for the past seven years it has appeared at the Bodega Bay Fisherman’s Festival. The band plays each year at the Sacramento Jazz Jubilee in Old Town during June. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band to open Piedmont’s 55th annual 4th of July Parade on Highland Avenue.

articles.text: Four years ago, near the start of freshman year of high school, I read a sentence that stood out. One sentence that I couldn’t get out of my head; a sentence that I think is relevant now and will be relevant for as long as I live. Now, before I say what I read, I want everyone to think back, let’s say four years ago, 2018, when you started freshman year. Think about who you were, what you believed, what you did, and what you said. Think about how others perceived you and, more importantly, how you perceived yourself. Now I want you to reflect on everything that has changed since then. I am willing to bet that there are a great number of things that you think now that you would not have thought before and things you said back then that you would not say now. In the past four years I have truly become much more grateful for my parents and friends for always being there to help and support me. The ability to change is one of the most beauPiedmont High School’s Class of 2022 Valedictorian Aaron Drumm tiful parts of life. So, why does it sometimes feel like your brain is sitting there fighting you saying, “Nope! You are not going to change that because we have been doing it this way our whole life.” And why is it that after making the decision to change, you can be called a hypocrite for doing something differently or believing something new? Why is it that changing is often so hard? Overcoming this opposite pull to change, this change inertia, is crucial to moving forward. The sentence I read, in Brandon Sanderson’s book, Oathbringer, that helped me realize this was, “Sometimes a hypocrite is nothing more than a man in the process of changing.” Among us, everyone here has been a hypocrite at some point. But you cannot let the label of being a hypocrite or being an imposter pull you down. Like Jacob and Wesley said, don’t be afraid to put yourself out there to make a change in the world – and within yourself. Don’t be held down by anything or anyone saying you can’t. Change is a journey that should never end, and as we overcome our own change inertia in order to move forward today, I want to leave everyone with one last quote. Coming from the same book, Sanderson writes, “The most important step a person can take is always the next one.” So today, when you get your diploma, take that next step, and stay in motion!

Think about who you were, what you believed, what you did, and what you said. Think about how others perceived you and, more importantly, how you perceived yourself. I am willing to bet that there are a great number of things that you think now that you would not have thought before and things you said back then that you would not say now. articles.text: Heat, Insulation, and reactions. Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions, When a s’more waffle cone is placed into a fire, heat (or energy) is transferred from the fire to the waffle cone. The additional heat raises the temperature, which can cause the ingredients inside to react and transform. As the temperature rises above a certain threshold, ingredients inside reach their melting point. Those that begun as solid ingredients begin to break down into less-than-solid states. This is why the ingredients begin to melt, mix, and become gooey! Adding foil around the waffle cones helps with the heating and melting process. Aluminum foil contains metal and therefore, acts as an insulator. This means it helps trap heat closer around the waffle cone, distributing the heat more evenly. Even though s’mores may seem like a simple, summer activity, they involve a lot of science that goes unseen. In this activity, learners will make s’mores using waffle cones and ingredients of their choosing. They will predict and observe how the heat and insulation of the cooking process transforms their cone into a melty, gooey, snack. Then, they will enjoy the results! This activity is fit for learners of all ages. Background information can be found at the end of this guide. PROCEDURE 1. Start by gathering around the campfire (or oven) and observing what happens when you place a single marshmallow into the heat. a. What do you notice happening to the marshmallow? b. Why do you think it is reacting that way? c. What do you think a marshmallow is made of that causes it to look/move/ react like that? 2. After making observations, pass out waffle cones and fill them with ingredients of your choice. 3. Make a few different cones. Fill one with classic ingredients, then experiment with different flavors, textures, and layers in the rest. 4. Once assembled, wrap it with foil. 5. Place them in the coals of a campfire and let it cook for about 5 to 7 minutes. a. If using the oven, bake them for 5 to 7 minutes at 400 degrees Fahrenheit. 6. While they’re cooking, make some predictions about your cones: a. What do you think the texture of each will be like? b. Which kinds of flavors do you think we will taste? c. The azure-blue coastline has been the playground of the rich since the Brits believed the sea air cured consumption (tuberculosis). It was previously a coastline of impoverished villagers who fished and farmed for a living, but when the Nice-Paris train route opened in the 1860s, English aristocrats infused wealth and built luxury villas. Ancient paths became roads cut from the great walls of rock from the southern flank of the Alps, which abruptly rises from the eastern shoreline. The Greeks were swept out by the Romans around 150 BCE, and when Rome fell in 476 A.D., the Goths defended the coastline. pages.text: Wednesday, June 15, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. IZZY EPSTEIN Softball Piedmont High Class of 2022 Chapman University Class of 2026 Izzy Epstein heads to Chapman University after earning The Post’s Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year. She was the WACC Shoreline’s Pitcher of the Year this spring after posting an impressive 12-1 record, with a 1.36 ERA, 123 innings pitched, and 187 strikeouts. She finished the season with 15 complete games, threw a perfect game on May 6 against Hayward, and recorded an astonishing 19 strikeouts in Piedmont’s 10-1 win over Arcata in the first round of the North Coast Section playoffs. She led the team to an 18-7 overall record and a perfect 10-0 against Shoreline teams on their way to a league title when they defeated Encinal 8-5 on May 12. On offense, she batted .368 with 25 hits and four home runs. Epstein was also named Honorable Mention by the Post as Freshman of the Year and Sophomore of the Year in 2020. What is your workout program this summer? Weight training and endurance conditioning three days a week with a trainer. I’ll also be doing hitting and throwing drills two days a week, practicing with a pitching coach once a week, and spot appearances on tournament softball teams throughout the summer. What are your fitness goals for this summer? Increase my strength and athletic coordination. I want to be prepared to step up to competitive college athletic fitness levels. How are you measuring your development? Weight levels on exercises like leg press, hip thrusts, kettle balls. In addition, I’ll measure my fastball velocity via radar gun and feedback from my pitching coach, Rich Balswick. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? All of the above. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? Increasing my pitch velocity by about 5 percent into the high 50s. Also, after having no homeruns through my first three years on varsity, I had four this year. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Dedicating yourself to training is a mindset. If you can stay dedicated for about the first 45 days, it gets a lot easier to train, workout, and practice since it becomes part of the fabric of your weeks. The only bad workout is no workout. articles.text: Eight Piedmont teenagers participated in the 27th annual U.S. Rowing Youth National Championship Regatta from June 9-12 in Sarasota, Florida. The prestigious event attracted over 3,500 student-athletes from hundreds of teams across the U.S. to compete in 34 different boating events. To qualify for the Junior Nationals, three Piedmont athletes with Oakland Strokes, two from Artemis Rowing, and another three from the OARS organization, had successful topfour performances weeks earlier at the Southwest Regional Championships at Lake Natoma near Sacramento. PHS graduating senior and soon-to-be St. Lawrence University rower Max Cole, a member of the Strokes, was part of the coxless quad boat with a winning time of 6:19.244. They edged out the second place boat from Marina Aquatic Center of Los Angeles by just 0.6 of a second. Cole will row for St. Lawrence University next fall. Jackson Violich, who just finished his sophomore year at PHS, was a member of the Strokes’ U-17 eight boat, which placed 8th and was second of six boats in the B Final. They clocked a 6:24.434 in Saturday’s final, less than a boat length behind Row New Jersey of Mount Arlington. Ali Gallacher, an incoming Piedmont junior, was a member of the Strokes’ coxed four boat, which finished 11th overall. It was fifth in the B Final on Sunday with a time of 7:29.7. Piedmont High School freshman Anna Lavin (top right) and Corpus Christi senior Isabella Warner (2nd from top right), members of Artemis Rowing. qualified for Junior Nationals in their coxed quad scull. Two Piedmont High students, Aaron Feldhammer (left) and Chris Fung (second from left), members of the OARS rowing organization. earned third-place finishes on quad scull. behind 2nd place Nereid Boat Club of Rutherford, New Jersey. The race was won by Maritime Rowing Club of Norwalk, Connecticut. PHS sophomore Zachary Feldstein, a member of OARS, placed 15th in single sculls. He was third in the C Final with a time of 7:52.632, a boat length back of second-place Eban Tracy of Washington’s Vashon Island Rowing Club and two boat lengths ahead of fourth-place Nikola Antich of Bergen County Rowing Academy of New Jersey. Artemis Rowing of Oakland also had two Piedmont teens at the Junior Nationals. PHS incoming sophomore Anna Lavin, and Isabella Warner, a recent graduate at Corpus Christi School, finished 14th in the coxed quad, and second of eight boats in the C Final with a time of 8:03.31, two seconds back of Atomic Rowing of Tennessee. Lavin and Warner’s boat narrowly missed out on the semifinals after finishing 13th in Thursday’s time trial in 7:55.5, just 1.1 second back of the 12th-place qualification. Less than one-third of a mile in, the mammoth tree begins to creep into sight behind your right shoulder. Leona Heights is among the best small treasures of Oakland, where you can find sprawling trees and a thriving babbling brook of Horseshoe Creek along the York Trail. articles.text: San Francisco Symphony has released a concert film of Igor Stravinsky’s The Soldier’s Tale as part of its free video streaming service, SFSymphony+. The film is Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen’s signature digital project released for the 2021-22 season. “The Soldier’s Tale has a very interesting place in history because it represents a complete change of paradigm,” said Salonen. “The opulent post-Romantic, late-Romantic era has come to a very violent and abrupt end: the world has experienced the first World War, the world has experienced a pandemic, and the new art looks very different, and sounds very different. It deals with contemporary issues, sometimes in an allegorical way, and there’s a sort of an ironic and distant approach to things. The Soldier’s Tale is thoroughly modern, and it represents the new era.” The Soldier’s Tale features actor Bruce Davison as the narPhoto by Kristen Loken Behind the scenes during filming of Stravinsky’s “The Soldier’s Tale.” rator, soldier, and devil; Alonzo King ballet dancer Adji Cissoko; and seven San Francisco Symphony musicians: Concertmaster Alexander Barantschik, Principal Bass Scott Pingel, Principal Clarinet Carey Bell, Principal Bassoon Stephen Paulson, Associate Principal Trumpet Aaron Schuman, Principal Trombone Timothy Higgins, and Principal Percussion Jacob Nissly. “I’ve always wanted to do a proper studio production of Soldier’s Tale, because it’s one of my favorite pieces and deserves a very well-thought-out, detailed production,” said Salonen. “Between the fact that it represents a new era in composition – and in the arts more generally – coupled with the Influenza pandemic, which was a big factor in driving all these changes, you cannot help but to draw parallels between that and our time. A hundred years earlier, Stravinsky was going through the same experiences in his life as we are now in our lives, and that’s almost spooky.” Visit https://www.sfsymphonyplus.org to access the film. Streaming is available on multiple devices.
articles.title: SF Symphony’s The Soldier’s Tale now streaming

articles.text: Festival Napa Valley, now in its 16th season, opens on July 15 with a wide range of concerts, concluding on July 24 with a finale concert by Festival Orchestra Napa. Concerts will be outdoors at several locations – the Festival Napa Valley Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, the Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at the Culinary Institute of America at Copia in Napa, and at wineries, estates and other venues throughout Napa Valley. articles.text: Mendocino Music Festival returns live this summer, beginning July 9 at Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg. Established in 1986 by Allan Pollack, Susan Waterfall and former principal bassoonist of the San Francisco Symphony, Walter Green, the festival features a blend of genres. The film is Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen’s signature digital project released for the 2021-22 season. “The Soldier’s Tale has a very interesting place in history because it represents a complete change of paradigm,” said Salonen. “The opulent post-Romantic, late-Romantic era has come to a very violent and abrupt end: the world has experienced the first World War, the world has experienced a pandemic, and the new art looks very different, and sounds very different. It deals with contemporary issues, sometimes in an allegorical way, and there’s a sort of an ironic and distant approach to things. The Soldier’s Tale is thoroughly modern, and it represents the new era.” The Soldier’s Tale features actor Bruce Davison as the narPhoto by Kristen Loken Behind the scenes during filming of Stravinsky’s “The Soldier’s Tale.” rator, soldier, and devil; Alonzo King ballet dancer Adji Cissoko; and seven San Francisco Symphony musicians: Concertmaster Alexander Barantschik, Principal Bass Scott Pingel, Principal Clarinet Carey Bell, Principal Bassoon Stephen Paulson, Associate Principal Trumpet Aaron Schuman, Principal Trombone Timothy Higgins, and Principal Percussion Jacob Nissly. “I’ve always wanted to do a proper studio production of Soldier’s Tale, because it’s one of my favorite pieces and deserves a very well-thought-out, detailed production,” said Salonen. “Between the fact that it represents a new era in composition – and in the arts more generally – coupled with the Influenza pandemic, which was a big factor in driving all these changes, you cannot help but to draw parallels between that and our time. articles.text: Violinist (and actress) Jayne Mansfield. Sex and violence. That’s what’s in the news. The news mongers assure us that’s what sells. Since the public demands it, I must concur. But look at the title of the column again. This article is about sex and VIOLINS. Let’s look back at some Hollywood history. Does anyone remember one of the greatest sex symbols of all time… Jayne Mansfield? There is a lot more to her than meets the eye (so to speak). Much that follows will surprise you. When I told my sister-in-law, Susan Hirshfield, that I intended to write an article about Jayne Mansfield, she related the following story. “I was 15 and in my first job at the famed May Company at the corner of Fairfax and Wilshire Boulevard in Los Angeles. The store received a call from Jayne Mansfield’s agent that she was coming to the store to shop. Everybody was told to show up. This was Hollywood, after all. I remember standing on the mezzanine of that amazing department store waiting for the show. Jane and her entourage finally swept in a good half hour later than she was supposed to arrive. All the photographers and other attendees were trailing behind her, including her little boy, who was about 10. The child was dressed in a Little Lord Fauntleroy costume… lace collar and all. The child looked positively humiliated. Jayne, wearing a remarkably tight dress, moved around conspicuously; the cameras flashing all the while. She went to the perfume counter and sampled a few while waving at people, and then she turned around and left just as quickly. The staff went back to work, feeling a bit downhearted about that poor little boy.” This vivid account is just a small part of a very big story that was Jayne Mansfield. But she was much more than just a publicity agent’s dream. The next part might surprise you very much. Another friend, who knew her, remarked on her disarming intelligence. In reality, Mansfield’s IQ was 163. She was a linguist and spoke five languages fluently. In addition to English she spoke French, Spanish, German, and Italian. I knew that she played the violin rather well. With a little bit of research, I found examples of her violin solos on YouTube. She played quite well. Jack Benny is remembered as being a very serious violinist, which he was. Jayne Mansfield was a much better player than Jack Benny. And she also played the piano. The Academy Awards ceremony has deteriorated in recent years. Back in 1958 an orchestra was formed to perform at the Academy Awards. Some of the musicians in the orchestra were some of the most famous Hollywood personalities. Dick Powell, who was a very fine singer, was the trumpet player. Hollywood tough guy Robert Mitchum played woodwinds. Elegant Fred Astaire was the drummer. Comedian Jerry Lewis conducted the band. Two famous Hollywood personalities who were notable for their absence were conductor Danny Kaye and singer extraordinaire Gloria Swanson. And yes, in that orchestra, Jayne Mansfield was the featured violinist. That was some orchestra! You will surprise yourselves by doing your own research on the musical talent named above. Even in death, Jayne Mansfield was a publicity agent’s dream. She was killed in an automobile accident on June 29, 1967. The headlines were exaggerated, but the tragedy was real. There are certain constants that we must remember in art. Look beneath the glitz. You might be surprised by genuine talent.

By Jim Gleason It’s hard to make a living as a musician, especially a black musician. Imagine trying to do so during the Great Depression. Charlie Christian was 13 when the Depression started and he died in 1942, three years after it ended. He was only 26. Under the direction of their blind father, Clarence Henry Christian, Charlie and his elder brothers Edward and Clarence would play in wealthier neighborhoods of their Oklahoma City hometown for cash or supplies. Charlie first entertained by dancing. Later, he learned trumpet, piano, then guitar. Electric guitar pioneer Eddie Durham said of Charlie: “We met in an Oklahoma City pool hall… Charlie was only playing a little piano then. He wasn’t playing guitar yet. He asked me to give him some pointers, like what to do if you want to play with class and get through life with the instrument. He wanted to know technical things, like how to pick a certain way. So I showed him the way to sound like I did. I said, ‘Don’t ever use an upstroke, which makes a taga-tag-a-tag sound; use a downstroke. It takes an awful fast wrist to play a downstroke— it gives a staccato sound, with no legato, and you sound like a horn.’ ” Eddie Durham also inspired Charlie to use a guitar amplifier. Brother Edward led a band as a pianist in Oklahoma City. Edward’s guitarist, Ralph Hamilton, taught Charlie how to play Sweet Georgia Brown, Rose Room, and Tea for Two. He played them at a jam session and was well-received. He jammed with notable performers including legendary jazz pianists Teddy Wilson and Art Tatum. articles.text: It was another beautiful, warm day for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group when they met on June 6 outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. Participating were Laura Goldman, Martin Levy, Jerry Gragg, Darby Gragg, Sarah Johnson, Adrienne Hamlin, Pat McMahon, Phil Witte, Dick Carter, Melba Yee, Ken Young, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The readers had selected The Body, a non-fiction book by British-American author Bill Bryson, who takes readers on a head-totoe, comprehensive tour of the human body, how it functions, its remarkable ability to heal itself, the ways it can fail, and ultimately how its passenger dies. The story is filled with extraordinary facts, such as your body made a million red blood cells since you started reading this. The book provides the reader with a deeper understanding of the miracle that is life in general, and you in particular. Bryson says that each of us is a walking, talking catalogue of wonders. “And how do we celebrate the glory of our existence?” Bryson asks. “Well, for most of us by exercising minimally and eating maximally.” After all Bryson’s collection of amazing facts, the ultimate conclusion of his book is a simple prescription for better life: eat a little bit less, move a little bit more. To the mild surprise of the group, the discussion was lively one that not only covered the book, but also took off on related topics. Martin Levy got the discussion started by sharing that long ago he read a 1968 book also titled The Body, this one by Anthony Smith. Priscilla Wanerus said that book sparked an interest that led to her having a career in the medical industry. Martin said he found the differences between what society found medically important then and now to be interesting. What people died from 50 years ago, compared to today is different and interesting. Most of the readers found that Bryson made the science of our personal, physical worlds both understandable and entertaining. He moved the readers through the book’s 464 pages with jokes, factoids, and biographical information that made reading a book about science enjoyable. Bryson is a good storyteller. Each chapter deals with a different part of our bodies. It was noted that at the end of them, Bryson wrote about what we still don’t know about how and why this or that part of us works the way it does. The readers then turned to future book selections. They had previously picked Cloud Cuckoo Land by Pulitzer-prize-winning fiction author Anthony Doerr for July, and The Chancellor, a biography of contemporary German chancellor Angela Merkel by Kati Marton for August. The group then selected Magpie Murders, a 2016 mystery novel by British author Anthony Horowitz, for September. Since the first Monday in July is July 4th, the next discussion will be Monday, July 11 at 1:30 p.m. outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, Registration is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Cloud Cuckoo Land by Anthony Doerr is the July pick.

For the past 20 years he has worked for Wilson Family Wines and is responsible for winemaking at multiple wineries. articles.text: A tiger-hybrid was rescued by Oakland Zoo from a roadside attraction in Oklahoma on Friday, June 10. Four big cats will now live safe, dignified lives after a cross-country rescue facilitated on June 10 by Oakland Zoo and two other animal organizations. The Zoo and globally accredited big cat sanctuaries Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge from Eureka Springs, Arkansas, and Lions, Tigers, and Bears in Alpine, California, teamed up to rescue a lion, a tiger hybrid and two tigers from a defunct, abandoned drive-thru roadside zoo offering cub petting and photo opportunities in northeast Oklahoma. The roadside attraction was cited and shut down by the USDA in 2008 for multiple animal safety and welfare violations. Its owner was reported to have ties to “Joe Exotic” from the Netflix series “Tiger King.” The rescue operation was initiated by Oakland Zoo, which was first contacted for help by a concerned Oklahoma resident last month. The concerned individual knew the defunct roadside zoo had four big cats that had been abandoned and were in poor condition. Colleen Kinzley, VP of Animal Care, Conservation and Research for Oakland Zoo, contacted two animal sanctuaries to team together in the effort. Oakland Zoo and Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge traveled to the defunct roadside zoo and conducted the onsite animal evaluations earlier this month. Funded by Oakland Zoo, the critical cross-country journey for the three tigers began with the help of a state-of-the-art animal rescue hauler owned by Lions, Tigers, and Bears. One tiger and the tiger-hybrid, now named “Lola” and “Mia” by the animal care team, arrived in Oakland on Sunday morning, June 12, and were transferred to the Zoo’s veterinary hospital for evaluation. “For the past 30 years, we’ve fully committed Oakland Zoo’s tiger habitat as a sanctuary for tigers victimized by the circus, roadside zoo, private ownership, and cub-petting industries. Those tigers need help, and we can provide that help while educating the public about the dangers of animal exploitation practiced in those industries,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. The rescued big cats, all female and some declawed, a standard practice in the cub-petting industry, include: • An elderly, arthritic lioness subjected to solitude for seven years. She required immediate medical attention and care. She is now at Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge. • A tiger-hybrid in poor condition with bowed legs and a badly infected tooth that has caused facial deformity, is now at Oakland Zoo. • Two tigers in separate enclosures, both energetic, but lean. One is now at Oakland Zoo and one is at Lions, Tigers & Bears. “Most likely, these cats were bred to be photo props, and once they grew too big and couldn’t be profitable, they were abandoned. We’re the animals’ voices, and we need to work toward education and legislation, because each animal rescued makes a difference,” said Bobbi Brink, founder and director of Lions, Tigers & Bears. Oakland Zoo’s tiger habitat features climbing platforms, two pools for swimming, trees, and a grass-covered ground. The tigers will receive four weeks of medical attention and care at the Zoo’s veterinary hospital before moving to the Zoo’s tiger habitat.
articles.title: Oakland Zoo helps rescue four big cats

The theme meant plenty of horseshoe games were played through a week in which they also made pinhole cameras and leather neckerchief slides. A favorite activity among the campers turned them into scientists, as they recorded the fantastic results of inserting mentos into a 2-liter bottle of Coca-Cola. Friendly sporting matches on the lawn and “banana tag” kept the kids running around all afternoon. There were three age-divided dens this year, each making a flag and a den cheer. After practicing all week, the campers recited their cheers in front of the entire camp. The youngest group of campers named themselves the “Avocado Ninjas”, while other dens took on the names “Turtles” moniker and “Bob is a Buffalo.” By the end of camp, the cub scouts were nearly professional in raising the flag, reciting the pledge of Allegiance, and Scouts Oath and the Scout Law. On the final day of camp, June Families took advantage of the shade on the blistering hot Friday, June 10, before watching the Cub Scout Day Camp’s Egg Drop. Piedmont Firefighter Paramedic Brian Protheroe descends from the 75-foot ladder during the Cub Scout Egg Drop on June 10 the egg drop. Kindergarten graduate, Barrett Williamson, holds up his egg capsule which easily floated back to earth like a feather. On a windless day, this egg gently floated down to the Dracena Park grass to the roar of the crowd. 10, the Scouts were presented with a special visit by the Piedmont Fire Department. Each Scout created a landing capsule (crash container) to hopefully allow their raw eggs to survive the 75-foot drop from the top of the fire engine ladder to the lawn of Dracena Park. After all 16 egg capsules were dropped, the Scouts could hardly contain their excitement to see the results. One by one the fate of each egg was revealed by the Scout leaders. Grand cheers went up for every surviving egg and applause reigned down for every successful Scout as they collected their rewards, a Mulberry’s coupon for a free ICEE. 2nd grader Sam Malione proudly holds the flag made by the Turtles Den. A camp favorite, Banana tag, involves freeze tag, and rock, paper, scissors. After Scout leaders secured the halyard and presented the colors, the flag was raised at the start of each day of the Cub Scout camp at Dracena Park. Campers eagerly awaited the opening of their egg drop containers after the drop.

State law requires cities to update their General Plan Housing Element. The City of Piedmont Draft Housing Element for the 6th Cycle (2023 - 2031) (“Draft Housing Element”) is part of the City’s General Plan and applies City-wide. The Draft Housing Element provides a plan for addressing housing needs over the next 8 years. The proposed Draft Housing Element has been developed to meet the State of California’s legal requirements, including the requirement to plan for the City’s share of the regional housing needs allocation (“RHNA”). The City of Piedmont is in the process of developing a programmatic and comprehensive Environmental Impact Report (“EIR”) in accordance with the California Environmental Quality Act for the Draft Housing Element. The EIR will be considered for certification in conjunction with the City’s final certification of the Housing Element. The Draft Housing Element is available for public review on the City’s web page at https://piedmont.ca.gov as well as https://piedmontishome.org. It is also available at City Hall, located at 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611, between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. On May 12, 2022, the Planning Commission recommended that the City Council direct staff to send the Draft Housing Element to HCD for its 90-day review.
